- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.75) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly to avoid overshoot.
- When sentiment is strongly negative (≤ -0.75), model often underestimates; adjust upward to reflect risk aversion or market recovery.
- Model frequently overreacts to recent spikes (e.g., +2–3% in 1–2 days), leading to over-forecasted peaks; apply smoothing or lagged decay to correct for momentum bias.
- If true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., price drops after a spike), model often fails to correct; apply downward bias in subsequent forecasts if sentiment is neutral or slightly negative.
- For 30-day horizon, model tends to overestimate in early days (1–5) when sentiment is volatile; reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5% for first 3–5 days if sentiment is mixed or trending.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “high-low” oscillations, model often misjudges mean reversion; use sentiment-weighted moving average to anchor forecasts near recent 7–14 day average.
- When sentiment is consistently positive but price declines (e.g., 0.5–1.5% drop over 3–5 days), model may overcorrect; reduce forecast by 0.2–0.8% to avoid “sell-off” overreaction.
